The fossa (Cryptoprocta ferox) is Madagascar's largest endemic carnivore, and its reproductive biology exhibits several striking features that set it apart from other euplerids. Females give birth to a single litter each year [F_R_i = single litter each year], typically comprising three pups per litter [N_R_i = three pups per litter]. This modest annual reproductive output is consistent with a relatively slow life-history pace for a mammal of its size. Gestation is completed over a period of 90 days [tg = 90 days] when individuals are maintained at 37.9 °C [T = 37.9 °C], a duration that reflects the constraints of embryonic development within a somewhat basal metabolic regime for a carnivore of moderate body mass. The neonatal pups, which are born in a relatively altricial state, weigh approximately 230 grams [Wwb = approximately 230 grams] at birth. This initial birth mass is quite modest compared to the ultimate size the animals will attain, representing only a small fraction of the adult weight that these predators will eventually achieve as they mature.

Following a brief period of intensive parental care, the altricial young undergo a critical transition to nutritional independence. The pre-weaning juvenile stage, during which the pups remain entirely dependent on the mother's milk, lasts for 129 days [tx = 129 days] at the species' typical core body temperature of 37.9 °C [T = 37.9 °C]. This weaning period is comparatively extended for a carnivore of this body size, likely reflecting the energetic challenges of provisioning offspring in the seasonal and resource-limited forests of Madagascar. The slow pace of early development is probably linked to the region's unpredictable prey base, which necessitates a prolonged period of maternal investment before the young are capable of securing their own food. By the time weaning is complete, the juvenile animals have undergone substantial somatic growth, but they remain many months away from attaining full body size and reproductive capability.

The protracted developmental trajectory continues well beyond weaning, as young fossas require a substantial interval to reach sexual maturity. Puberty is not attained until approximately 1496 days after birth [tp = approximately 1496 days after birth] when the animals are maintained at the typical body temperature of 37.9 °C [T = 37.9 °C]. This remarkably late age at sexual maturation, exceeding four years, is one of the most extreme among placental carnivores of comparable weight and may reflect a combination of intense intraspecific competition for territory and the need to acquire formidable hunting skills before undertaking reproduction. The long delay before the onset of gonadal activity allows individuals to achieve near-maximal skeletal and muscular development, which is critical for a species that relies on subduing prey such as lemurs. This life-history strategy, characterized by a slow and steady accumulation of body mass, contrasts sharply with the faster-paced reproductive schedules seen in many mainland carnivorans.

As a result of this extended developmental schedule, the overall lifespan of the fossa is relatively long for a carnivore of its size. The maximum recorded longevity in captivity has been documented at 23.1 years [am = 23.1 years] when the animals are housed under thermoneutral conditions of 37.9 °C [T = 37.9 °C]. Such a lifespan, spanning over two decades, is consistent with a slow life-history continuum marked by low annual fecundity and a late onset of reproduction. In the wild, actual longevity is likely somewhat shorter due to the pressures of disease, injury, and resource scarcity, but the species' capacity for extended survival is evident. This long potential lifespan allows for multiple reproductive attempts across a female's lifetime, partially compensating for the low annual litter output. The combination of a single yearly litter and infrequent pulses of parturition means that each individual offspring represents a substantial parental investment.

Adult body size in the fossa is sexually dimorphic, with males typically attaining a larger ultimate body mass than females. Females generally reach an adult wet weight on the order of 5500 to 8600 grams (5500-8600 grams) [Wwi = 5500-8600 grams], whereas the heavier males can attain a maximum size as high as 11 kilograms [Wwi = 11 kilograms]. This sexual size dimorphism is thought to be linked to male-male competition for access to estrous females during the breeding season. The wide range in reported adult weights, from approximately 5.5 to 12 kg, reflects the species' considerable geographic and individual variation across the fragmented landscapes of Madagascar. The substantial difference between the minimal neonatal mass of about 230 grams and the ultimate adult mass, which may exceed 11 kilograms, underscores the remarkable degree of somatic growth that these animals undergo during their prolonged period of maturation.

The fossa's ecological role as a top predator on Madagascar has likely shaped its unusual life-history traits. The species occupies a unique niche, preying primarily on lemurs, and this dietary specialization may impose strong selective pressures on body size and developmental timing. The combination of a relatively low reproductive rate, an extended period of maternal care, and a late age at sexual maturity is reminiscent of other island carnivores that evolved in environments with limited prey diversity and reduced competition. The fossa's life-history strategy, characterized by high parental investment per offspring and a long potential lifespan, aligns with a slow-paced life-history continuum that is more typical of larger-bodied mammals than of species in the 5 to 12 kilogram body mass range.
